extracted.intended_audience: lawyers, judges, and law students working on U.S. patent litigation (pleading and defenses)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedural rules for asserting and defending claims in actions at law on U.S. patents, focusing on which defenses require special pleas, demurrers, evidence, and the effect of estoppel and statutes of limitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambiguous or nebulous claims defence (specification deceptive)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Where a specification, by ambiguity and a needless multiplication of nebulous claims, is calculated to deceive and mislead the public, the patent is void."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This defence may be made by demurrer because validity against it is a question of construction of the letters patent themselves, though a special plea is probably the best means of interposing it; less meritorious necessity for special pleading than for other defences which assail validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fourteenth defence — claiming both new and old invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a new invention and an old one are both claimed in a patent, the patentee may sustain an action on the former only if he disclaims the latter without unreasonable delay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether the old invention was old and whether delay to disclaim was unreasonable are matters of fact depending on evidence; this defence therefore requires a special plea to bring it into the action at law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fifteenth defence — jurisdiction of Commissioner to reissue
rubrics_metrics.description: A defence attacking the Commissioner's jurisdiction to reissue the patent in suit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Questions of its applicability are mainly questions of fact depending on evidence in pais; a special plea is the proper means of bringing it to the court's attention (see chapter on reissues).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sixteenth defence — broadened reissue (timing and comparison with original)
rubrics_metrics.description: Defence based on the relation between the original and the reissue: comparison of claims/contents and the particular length of time between original and application for reissue which may be fatal to a broadened reissue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plaintiff suing on a reissue need not introduce the original in evidence; defendant must prove contents of the original. The materiality of time lapse is a variable, circumstance-dependent question of fact; special plea is proper to notify plaintiff what must be met at trial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seventeenth defence — reliance on proof of the original patent
rubrics_metrics.description: A defence that depends upon proof of the original patent and thus requires at least that amount of evidence to support it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where sameness or difference of invention is complicated, courts may require evidence; to give both sides opportunity to produce such evidence, a special plea seems necessary, although some cases have held a general denial of the declaration to be enough.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eighteenth defence — confession and avoidance; demurrer possible in some cases
rubrics_metrics.description: A defence in confession and avoidance which in cases based on the prior patent may be made by demurrer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In cases founded on the prior patent a demurrer may suffice; in other cases it requires a special plea because it is in confession and avoidance of the declaration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nineteenth defence — defence based on repeal of the patent
rubrics_metrics.description: A defence asserting that the patent was repealed by a court record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requires evidence of the record of the court which repealed the patent. Because such record cannot be contradicted and its existence would be known to plaintiff or his privies, there seems no strong reason to insist on a special plea, though in absence of precedent filing a special plea is safest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Twentieth defence — expiration of a foreign patent on same invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Defence that a foreign patent on the same invention has expired, potentially limiting or defeating the U.S. patentee's suit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demands a special plea because proof of existence and expiration of the foreign patent comes from outside the U.S. patent in suit and generally requires expert testimony that the foreign patent is for the same invention. Defence may fail if the foreign patent was surreptitiously taken out by another without U.S. patentee's knowledge. Special plea gives plaintiff notice to meet such evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Twenty-first defence — must be negatived in declaration; available under general issue
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the defence is such that it must be negatived in the declaration, the defendant may make it under the general issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the declaration already negatives the fact, the defendant may raise the defence under the general issue rather than by a special plea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Twenty-second defence — attacking plaintiff's title vs paramount assignment
rubrics_metrics.description: Defence arguing that plaintiff's evidence fails to make out any title, or that plaintiff has no such title enabling him to sue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where defendant merely argues plaintiff's evidence is insufficient, the general issue suffices; but if defendant attacks title on basis of a paramount assignment to another, the defence ought to be pleaded specially to avoid surprising the plaintiff at trial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Twenty-third & twenty-fourth defences — historical special pleading requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: These defences traditionally required special pleading under ancient common law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although eighteenth-century English practice relaxed this (allowing proof under the general issue in ordinary cases), U.S. courts may not extend that relaxation to patent litigation; thus special pleading remains advisable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Twenty-fifth defence — general denial of infringement under general issue
rubrics_metrics.description: A defence consisting simply in a denial of the alleged infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The general issue is and always was appropriate for this defence. Even if a proper non-infringement defence involves evidence of the state of the art, the general issue is a sufficient plea because no notice to the plaintiff is necessary to render such evidence admissible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estoppel by matter of record (res judicata)
rubrics_metrics.description: Estoppel arising from prior adjudication (res judicata) which prevents relitigation of matters once finally decided between the same parties or those similarly connected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requires final judgment—interlocutory decrees do not suffice; binds parties and those who purchase interests after decree or who openly assume control/expense of former litigation; only questions actually litigated and decided are conclusive; mutuality and knowledge of participation may be required to bind third parties who assisted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estoppel by matter of deed (contracts, assignments, admissions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Estoppel arising from conveyance/contractual admissions where alleged infringer by contract admitted validity or agreed not to infringe, or an assignor/grantor later infringes what he conveyed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such persons are estopped from denying title or validity even if invalidity arose from unlawful reissue or known defects at assignment; estoppel extends to co-operating strangers and corporations formed by assignor, but generally not to mere employees or corporations which in good faith took over business without special reference to the patent; assignor still may show narrow construction unless he made representations of scope as inducement to sale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estoppel in pais / implied licenses
rubrics_metrics.description: Estoppels arising from conduct or representations (in pais) and implied licenses that may preclude assertion of patent rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estoppel in pais may operate similarly to implied licenses; earlier discussion connected it with implied licenses. The topic is complex and often requires resort to standard texts on estoppel for application in patent litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleading requirement for estoppel
rubrics_metrics.description: Estoppel must be specially pleaded to operate as a bar in subsequent litigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a former judgment or decree is not pleaded as an estoppel, the defendant refers the merits anew to the court; the former adjudication may be argued but cannot be relied on as a bar unless set up in a special plea.

rubrics_metrics.name: National statute of limitations for patent suits (six-year rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: Since 1898 there is a national statute providing that no money recovery may be had for any infringement committed more than six years before the beginning of such an action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This defence (statute of limitations) cannot be availed of upon the general issue and typically must be specially pleaded. The national statute preempts state statutes where it applies.

rubrics_metrics.name: State statutes of limitation and preemption
rubrics_metrics.description: State statutes of limitation cannot apply to patent rights that are subject to a national statute of limitations; state statutes of limitation for torts without force apply where no national statute governs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because states cannot control patent law and Congress has provided rules for Federal courts in these matters, national rules govern where enacted; absent a national statute, relevant state tort statutes of limitation may apply to infringement actions of a tortious character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Replications and subsequent pleadings (licenses, releases, limitations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Replications and subsequent pleadings are seldom required in patent cases because most pleas are in bar by traverse; principal exceptions are pleas of license, release, and statute of limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If plaintiff denies existence of a license or release, replication should be by way of traverse concluding to the country. If plaintiff alleges duress, fraud, or revocation, replication should be by confession and avoidance with verification, causing a rejoinder and possibly a sur-rejoinder; parties should traverse or plead confession and avoidance appropriately to tender issue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Similiter requirement when issue is tendered
rubrics_metrics.description: A similiter must be filed or added whenever either party properly tenders issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The similiter is a formal pleading that should always be attended to in common-law pleading; omission has sometimes been fatal, though it is largely a formality added for the party who is tendered issue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demurrer procedure and scope
rubrics_metrics.description: A demurrer may be interposed by either party to any pleading of opponent except another demurrer; when interposed, the court examines all pleadings and generally decides against the party who first filed a substantially defective one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demurrer to a declaration will not be sustained if the declaration is too large (contains an independent part good in law), while this exception does not apply to pleas, replications, or rejoinders which are entire; strategic considerations: vital defences should not be trusted solely to a demurrer unless certain it will not be overruled.

rubrics_metrics.name: When a declaration is demurrable
rubrics_metrics.description: Declarations are demurrable when the patent appears void on its face or by judicial notice, when necessary allegations are omitted, when allegations are in improper form, or when claimed infringement covers time barred portions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If declaration alleges infringement beginning more than six years before the suit and continuing past the limit, defendant may special demur to the divisible time-barred part; general demurrer to entire declaration will be overruled if an independent unbarred part remains.

rubrics_metrics.name: When pleas are demurrable
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleas are demurrable when facts stated constitute no defence, are in improper form, or when statute of limitation is pleaded to the whole of a right where only part is barred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A plea bad in part is bad altogether; use joinder in demurrer as proper response; filing formalities may be waived in practice but substantive defects remain fatal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joinder in demurrer and appellate consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: A joinder in demurrer is the proper response; if a party demurs and the opponent refuses to join, that party discontinues action or defence. When a demurrer to an entire declaration is sustained and cannot be cured, the plaintiff may appeal; if demurrer overruled, defendant may plead but loses right to later review of overruled demurrer on appeal if he elects to plead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical effect: do not trust a vital defence only to a demurrer unless you accept the strategic consequences of an overruled demurrer and lost appellate review of that point.
